transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-18
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim, Priya Desai, Marcus Liu, Nate R. (Redwood) -- Leah Ortiz, Ravi Menon, Sam Cho, Priya K, Jordan (Catalyst)

Summary:
Quick sync on the Catalyst POC focusing on prefix and KV prefetch strategies. Reviewed latest hit-rate numbers, discussed prompt reuse canonicalization, investigated a spike in tail latency tied to cold KV lookups, agreed on additional telemetry exports and a 24h synthetic run to stress the caching heuristics. Action items and next steps captured.

Topics:
- Live hit-rate dashboard review
- Cold vs warm KV lookup latency and eviction behavior
- Prompt normalization / canonicalization for reuse
- Prefetch strategy: LRU + time-window vs score-based prefetch
- Tradeoffs: latency headroom vs unit cost + dedicated burst capacity
- Benchmark plan for on-prem microbench

Action items (brief): see metadata section

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Kim: okay let's get started. thanks for hopping on, everyone. quick roll call?
[00:07] Leah Ortiz: Leah here. hi.
[00:09] Ravi Menon: Ravi here.
[00:11] Sam Cho: Sam, product.
[00:13] Priya K: Priya, NLP.
[00:15] Jordan: Jordan, data infra.
[00:17] Alex Kim: great. from Redwood side it's Alex, Priya (SE), Marcus (CSM) and Nate who will hop in for the bench later. we got 50 minutes, main goal is hit-rate review and decide next tuning steps.
[00:30] Priya Desai: quick preface — we pulled the latest CSV you uploaded last night and overlaid it with our prefix histogram. overall the KV hit-rate bumped from 32% to about 45% on weekday traffic after enabling the 2-token canonicalization rule. that was the low-hanging improvement.
[00:48] Leah Ortiz: yep that's what we saw in our internal dashboard too. curious about the tail though, there's still some 600ms tail tokens and that hurts our chat UI.
[00:57] Priya Desai: right. when we split traces the 95-99 percentile is dominated by cold KV lookups and longer tokenization mismatches. a lot of it is prompt variants: punctuation, casing, and the small HTML snippets the product app inserts.
[01:18] Sam Cho: can you define prompt variants, sorry? like are these user messages or system prompts?
[01:22] Priya K: mostly user messages and sometimes markup; we found users paste code blocks and sometimes include the same query with different whitespace, so the prefix key changes.
[01:34] Alex Kim: the canonicalization we used is intentionally conservative — strip repeated whitespace, normalize numbers, lower-case except for known proper names — this jumps reuse w/o over-normalizing.
[01:44] Ravi Menon: any risk of semantic collisions with that? we don't want different intents collapsed.
[01:50] Priya Desai: good question, yes there's always a false merge risk. we tested on a sample of 60k queries and only ~0.3% merged where downstream answer differed materially. we can tune thresholds and add a safelist for token sequences that must remain verbatim.
[02:12] Marcus Liu: quick interjection — we also added a prefetch window where the router will proactively warm a small set of next likely prefixes based on session history; that's reduced user-observed first-token latency by about 40ms in our internal sims.
[02:30] Jordan: how aggressive is prefetch? are we sending extra traffic to models? that's the cost question.
[02:35] Priya Desai: it's score-based: only prefetch top-3 predicted prefixes per session and only for sessions that historically had >50% reuse. we also debounce prefetches to avoid bursts.
[02:46] Leah Ortiz: that makes sense, but I saw CPU spikes in our infra when we had a burst of prefetches last test. could be our network config + route.
[02:57] Alex Kim: may be related to concurrent prefetch windows. we'll add jitter and a soft rate limit. also note Redwood routing can route prefetches to a lower-cost replica or cached variant to reduce model spend.
[03:14] Priya K: about the cold lookup tail: we instrumented the KV store and saw a pattern — cold misses were often for prefixes that had been evicted minutes earlier because they were sized to LRU with a low memory cap.
[03:26] Ravi Menon: what's our eviction policy right now? LRU per-shard?
[03:29] Priya Desai: yes, LRU per-shard with a per-shard target memory. we recommended switching to segmented LRU with a tiny protected L0 for high-frequency prefixes and a larger L1 for others; that preserved a lot of the hot ones in our tests.
[03:45] Sam Cho: segmented LRU sounds complex — operationally, who manages sizes?
[03:49] Priya Desai: Redwood can suggest defaults and tune based on observed prefix frequency. Primarily we'd export the frequency histogram and you tune the L0 proportion — it's not a hard requirement to run.
[03:59] Jordan: can we get that histogram?
[04:01] Priya Desai: yes, Alex will share link.
[04:05] Alex Kim: noted, will share. (typing) also we included per-request KV latency percentiles — the 99th during the spike hit ~610ms but median is 22ms. so it's concentrated.
[04:19] Leah Ortiz: that 610ms is what ends up blocking our UI render; even though average is low it kills UX.
[04:26] Marcus Liu: for UI-critical flows we recommend an inline fallback: stream partial tokens as soon as model returns first chunk and show a typing indicator when a secondary KV lookup completes.
[04:38] Sam Cho: hmm that may be fine, but it's more engineering on our side.
[04:42] Leah Ortiz: what's the alternative? raise the cache size?
[04:45] Priya Desai: yes you can increase memory for the KV layer or run a small dedicated slice with higher hit-rate guarantees. that's where dedicated capacity helps — predictable tail latency at a higher cost.
[04:57] Ravi Menon: cost numbers please — need to show to finance.
[05:00] Alex Kim: we'll include a rough delta for the dedicated slice: expect ~+30% on per-token infra cost but 2-3x improvement in 99th tail latency in our observed workloads. I'll send a short cost/latency comparison table.
[05:14] Priya K: one more point on prompt reuse: we recommend a two-pass lookup — first a strict prefix match for exact reuses, then a looser normalized-match for fuzzy reuse. that keeps precision high while capturing more savings.
[05:30] Jordan: does that double KV lookups? more ops = more latency?
[05:33] Priya Desai: we implemented it with client-side short-circuiting: if strict hits, we skip fuzzy. if strict misses, client does a single fuzzy lookup that is cached locally for the session to avoid repeated fuzzy ops.
[05:48] Leah Ortiz: what's the SDK effort for that? our team uses the JS SDK heavily.
[05:52] Alex Kim: small change — a single flag and a tiny canonicalization hook; Priya will open a PR template for your team to review.
[05:59] Sam Cho: on telemetry, can we get sample traces for the problematic requests? full traces not PII?
[06:04] Priya Desai: yes, we'll sanitize and strip PII. we'll include token-level timing and KV IDs for the requests.
[06:11] Alex Kim: okay let's talk bench plan: we propose a 24-hour synthetic run that reproduces your session skew (top 20% sessions generate 70% of traffic) and a 2-hour high-concurrency microbench for on-prem. results should show hit-rate evolution and tail latency.
[06:29] Ravi Menon: for on-prem microbench, we need to validate network topology and HSM/KMS interactions, that'll be a separate pre-checklist.
[06:36] Marcus Liu: Nate will coordinate the microbench and share the checklist after this call. Nate — you want to say briefly?
[06:41] Nate R.: yeah i'll drop a runbook: tests, env vars, expected artifacts. plan to run on Tuesday/Wednesday next week, unless you want earlier.
[06:49] Leah Ortiz: Tuesday works for us.
[06:51] Priya K: one quick anomaly we noticed: some prefixes had high reuse but low KV hit because the canonicalization produced slightly different tokens due to unicode normal forms — turned out some inputs used non-breaking spaces.
[07:03] Sam Cho: wow. do we have a list?
[07:05] Priya Desai: yes, the normalization docs will include that and a small set of unicode normalization rules to apply client-side.
[07:12] Alex Kim: ok near-term decisions: 1) share dashboard and histograms, 2) run 24h synthetic test, 3) microbench on-prem next Tues, 4) Redwood to export KV latency percentiles and cold-sample traces. any objections?
[07:27] Leah Ortiz: all good.
[07:30] Ravi Menon: good.
[07:31] Sam Cho: yep.
[07:33] Alex Kim: wrap-up: will send meeting notes, action items and a proposed pricing delta for dedicated slice. any last questions?
[07:40] Priya K: small ask — can you include examples of false-positive canonicalization cases?
[07:44] Priya Desai: yes we'll include a short appendix with about 20 examples and suggested safelist patterns.
[07:50] Alex Kim: thanks everyone. we'll follow up via email and slack. meeting adjourned.

End of transcript.
